reference.source: Standard endocrinology reference texts and adrenal disorder consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome in which both adrenal glands are enlarged by multiple non-pigmented macronodules, often discovered incidentally on imaging
Cortisol excess is frequently mild or subclinical, so many patients present with metabolic features (hypertension, glucose intolerance, obesity) rather than florid Cushingoid appearance
A hallmark is aberrant expression of illicit G-protein-coupled receptors on the adrenal cortex, causing cortisol secretion driven by non-ACTH signals
Food-dependent (GIP-mediated) hypercortisolism is the classic example, where meals rather than pituitary ACTH trigger cortisol release
Other aberrant receptors described include those responsive to vasopressin, catecholamines, LH/hCG, and serotonin, which can be probed with provocative testing
Plasma ACTH is suppressed and low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol, confirming an ACTH-independent adrenal source
Germline ARMC5 variants underlie a substantial proportion of apparently sporadic bilateral disease and warrant consideration of familial screening
reference.pathophysiology: The adrenal cortices become progressively enlarged by numerous benign macronodules that autonomously secrete cortisol independent of pituitary ACTH, which is consequently suppressed. A central mechanism is the aberrant (ectopic or over-expressed) presence of G-protein-coupled receptors on steroidogenic cells, so that ligands not normally driving cortisol, such as gastric inhibitory polypeptide released after meals, vasopressin, catecholamines or serotonin, inappropriately stimulate steroidogenesis. Local intra-adrenal production of ACTH by nodular cells may further sustain growth in a paracrine loop. Inactivating germline mutations in the tumour-suppressor ARMC5 are commonly identified and predispose to the multinodular bilateral phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with adrenal nodularity
additionalInvestigations: Late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing and paired plasma ACTH to establish ACTH independence
Cross-sectional adrenal imaging (CT or MRI) demonstrating bilateral macronodular enlargement
Provocative testing for aberrant receptor responses (e.g. mixed-meal, posture, and hormone challenge protocols)
ARMC5 germline genetic testing and family screening where indicated
Metabolic assessment for glucose intolerance, dyslipidaemia and bone density loss
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or severe hypercortisolism suggesting a more aggressive adrenal pathology
Imaging features atypical for benign hyperplasia raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma
Uncontrolled hypertension, hypokalaemia or diabetes reflecting significant hormone excess
Signs of adrenal insufficiency after unilateral or bilateral surgery
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually indolent with benign nodules, and metabolic and cortisol excess can be controlled by unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, though bilateral resection commits the patient to lifelong steroid replacement. Long-term outcome is generally good when hypercortisolism is corrected and associated cardiometabolic risk is managed.
pitfalls: Dismissing bilateral adrenal enlargement as non-functioning without screening for subclinical cortisol excess
Overlooking aberrant receptor-driven (e.g. food-dependent) cortisol secretion that can be targeted medically
Assuming the disease is sporadic and failing to consider ARMC5-related familial risk
Precipitating adrenal insufficiency by removing both glands without planning glucocorticoid replacement
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on adrenal Cushing syndrome
